01 · Research questionWhere does armed conflict concentrate, and is it moving?

Where do recorded conflict events form significant local clusters, and which township hotspots persist, emerge, intensify or weaken through time?

87,103 ACLED events recorded in the study period

330 Myanmar townships (MIMU Admin-3)

57 monthly time steps, Jan 2021 – Sep 2025

18,810 township-months in a complete space-time cube

Why it matters. Myanmar’s post-2021 conflict is geographically uneven. A national total hides where violence concentrates and how that concentration shifts, which is exactly what peace-building and humanitarian teams need in order to decide where to look first.

02 · Study area and dataA township-level view of Myanmar, 2021–2025

Total recorded events by township, Jan 2021 – Sep 2025 (quantile classes within each map)

Inputs

  • ACLED event points: date, type, coordinates, fatalities
  • MIMU Admin-3 township boundaries, P-code v9.4
  • Projected working copy in EPSG:6933 for geometry

Data-quality gates

  • 0 duplicate IDs, 0 missing dates or coordinates
  • 1,112 events missing a township name → assigned by coordinates
  • Only 9 of 87,103 points fall outside any township
  • Zero-event months kept as observed zeros

The burden is highest in the Sagaing–Magway dry zone (Yinmarbin 3,057 · Salingyi 2,038 · Kale 2,009 events), while battles peak in Shan and Kayin (Nawnghkio 447 · Kawkareik 441) and civilian harm also stands out in Myingyan (Mandalay) and Hpakant (Kachin).

03 · Analytical approachFrom event points to hotspot trajectories

1 Prepare & match Clean ACLED fields, audit precision, assign every event to a township P-code by spatial join. → township event table

2 Space-time cube Count events per township-month and complete all 330 × 57 combinations. → regular monthly series

3 Local association Local Moran’s I separates clusters from outliers; local Gi* finds high- and low-value concentrations. → LISA & Gi* maps

4 Conflict composition Repeat Gi* for all events, battles and violence against civilians under one rule. → hotspot agreement map

5 Change through time Monthly Gi* maps, Mann-Kendall trends and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis. → EHSA hotspot classes

Weights · Queen contiguity, row-standardised Gi* band · fixed 185.8 km Permutations · 99, seed 626 Decision rule · p < 0.05, with BH-adjusted check Software · R: sf, sfdep, tmap, Kendall

Local Moran’s I asks

Is a township similar to or different from its neighbours? It finds clusters (High-High) and outliers (Low-High).

Local Gi* asks

Is this area a significant concentration of high (hotspot) or low (cold spot) event counts?

EHSA asks

How has each township’s Gi* changed across 57 months: intensifying, oscillating, sporadic or diminishing?

04 · Key findingsFinding 2: The same hotspot can mean different kinds of violence

19
Shared hotspotHot for all events, battles and civilian violence: Yinmarbin, Salingyi, Monywa, Myaing, Yesagyo, Pauk.
14
Battle-led hotspotArmed confrontation dominates, mainly in Kayin, Magway and Mandalay.
13
Civilian-harm hotspotViolence against civilians stands out, mainly in Mandalay, Sagaing and Chin.
1
Battle-civilian overlapHot for both specific types but not for the aggregate count (Sagaing).

Takeaway. An aggregate hotspot map says where; the three-way comparison says what kind of violence drives it. Battle-led and civilian-harm areas call for different responses.

04 · Key findingsFinding 3: Hotspots move month to month

Significant monthly Gi* hotspots (red), Oct 2024 – Sep 2025, Queen contiguity

The last 12 months

  • Oct 2024 – Mar 2025: the Sagaing–Magway dry-zone corridor holds the main concentration.
  • Apr – May 2025: the focus shifts south-east to Kayin.
  • Jun – Sep 2025: it moves toward Mandalay, partly returns to the dry zone, then fragments.

Most persistent townships

7 of 12 months: Salingyi, Monywa, Pale, Singu
6 of 12 months: Pakokku, Myaing, Budalin, Yesagyo

The widest spread in the full 57 months was April 2023, with 30 hotspot townships at once.

05 · Public-safety implicationsTurning hotspot types into monitoring priorities

Hotspot signal Recommended response Why
Recurring recent hotspots
Salingyi, Monywa, Pale, Singu		 Sustained township-level review Hotspot in 7 of the last 12 months: the concentration keeps coming back, it is not a one-off spike.
Intensifying hotspots
Northern & southern Shan, Kawthoung		 Field verification and closer monitoring Local concentration is still rising, so the situation may be getting worse.
Sporadic & oscillating hotspots
Kachin, Rakhine, Bago, Mandalay		 Flexible, event-triggered monitoring Violence disappears and returns, so a fixed long-run ranking would miss flare-ups.
Civilian-harm hotspots
Mandalay, Sagaing, Chin		 Protection-focused programming Recorded violence targets civilians directly, not only armed actors.
Diminishing hotspots
Chipwi, Myitkyina, Pyay		 Follow-up before de-prioritising A falling statistic does not prove that present-day harm is low.

These maps are a screening tool, not a final decision. Field action should also weigh population exposure, displacement, access conditions and consultation with affected communities.

06 · LimitationsWhat the evidence can and cannot support

Data

  • ACLED records reflect reporting access; remote or restricted areas may be under-recorded.
  • Event counts measure recorded burden, not population risk.
  • 9 events could not be placed in a township.

Method

  • Township boundaries and monthly bins shape the clusters (MAUP).
  • With 99 permutations, p cannot fall below ~0.01, which limits BH resolution across 330 tests.
  • The 185.8 km Gi* band smooths broadly; Queen weights follow immediate neighbours.

Interpretation

  • Results show where and when concentration occurs, not why.
  • The 12-month maps are a display window; EHSA uses the full 57 months.
  • Nominal p < 0.05 follows the course workflow; BH counts are a stricter check.

Reproducible workflow. The Quarto technical report runs end-to-end with a fixed seed (626) and records data sources, CRS, parameters and every analytical decision.
